notes:
These notes cover Mark 1:23–45, but some verses have little or nothing. I ran out of searches and page reads, and the long pages (Enduring Word, the Gospel Coalition commentary, Precept Austin) came back cut off before this passage. So most of the notes come from search snippets. The thinnest verses are vv. 27–28, 32–33 and 36–39. I found nothing from Lutheran or Orthodox sources (lcms.org, 1517.org, oca.org) or from newadvent.org.

---

**v. 23**
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Mark describes the man as "with" (literally "in") an unclean spirit, using the same grammar Paul uses for being "in Christ." This unclean spirit was the evil lord of this poor man's life. Guzik warns that things like spiritism, astrology, occult practices and drugs can open doors to demons. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- **Matthew Henry:** The man was "in" the spirit the way someone is "in a fever," completely overcome by it. The devil is called unclean because he has lost all the purity of his nature, because he acts in direct opposition to the Holy Spirit of God, and because with his suggestions he pollutes the spirits of men. Henry adds that some think he came to oppose Christ, not to be taught or healed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_001.cfm
- **Strauss (TGC, Reformed):** "Spirit" here means a demon allied with Satan. Mark treats "demon" and "unclean spirit" as the same thing, and Strauss thinks a better rendering is "impure" or "defiling." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/mark/

**v. 24**
- **Henry:** Because the spirit was unclean, it hated and feared Christ, knowing Him to be holy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_001.cfm
- **William Kelly (StudyLight):** The man's voice and the demon's are strangely mixed together in "What have *we* to do with thee?" https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-41.html

**v. 25**
- **Henry:** "Be silent" literally means "be muzzled." Christ rejects such praise from a demon, whether it "fawns" or "barks." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_001.cfm
- **Strauss (TGC):** This is where Mark's "messianic secret" begins, the pattern of Jesus ordering people to keep quiet about who He is. Jesus silences demons to demonstrate his authority and to define his messiahship on his own terms. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/mark/

**v. 26**
- **Henry:** The spirit gives in because it has no choice. Unable to touch Christ, it lashes out in fury at the man with a violent convulsion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_001.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** Demons can cause physical affliction, convulsions included, but clearly not all physical affliction is demonic in origin. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/mark-1-commentary

**v. 27**
- **Henry:** As he taught, so he healed, with authority. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_001.cfm

**v. 28:** Nothing found.

**v. 29**
- **McGarvey (Bible Hub):** Peter and Andrew had lived in Bethsaida (John 1:44). They may have moved to Capernaum, or Bethsaida may be counted here as part of Capernaum. https://biblehub.com/library/mcgarvey/the_four-fold_gospel/xxxii_healing_peters_mother-in-law_and.htm

**v. 30: Protestants and Catholics differ on what this verse says about Peter's marriage**
- **Protestant reading:**
  - **GotQuestions:** We know for certain that Peter was married because he had a mother-in-law. It argues that clerical celibacy goes against the apostles' example. https://www.gotquestions.org/disciples-married.html
  - **McGarvey:** Those who call Peter the first pope must admit he was married, and he says celibacy has no support in Scripture. https://biblehub.com/library/mcgarvey/the_four-fold_gospel/xxxii_healing_peters_mother-in-law_and.htm
- **Catholic reading:**
  - **Catholic Answers:** Priestly celibacy is not an unchangeable dogma but a disciplinary rule, so a married Peter poses no problem for Catholic faith. https://www.catholic.com/tract/celibacy-and-the-priesthood
  - **Karl Keating:** Peter's wife is never mentioned at her sick mother's bedside. Keating thinks Peter was probably a widower by then. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/did-peter-have-a-wife
  - **Another Catholic Answers piece:** Whether she was still alive is an open question. https://www.catholic.com/qa/what-was-up-with-st-peters-wife

**v. 31**
- **Bible Hub Topical:** Her getting up at once to serve shows the healing was complete. Her service is a natural response of gratitude for grace received. https://biblehub.com/topical/p/peter's_mother-in-law.htm

**vv. 32–33:** Nothing beyond what is under v. 35.

**v. 34**
- **NET Bible note:** Some manuscripts expand "they knew Him" to "they knew Him to be the Christ." https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/download/netbible/ondemand/bybook/mar.pdf
- On silencing the demons, see Strauss under v. 25.

**v. 35**
- **J. D. Jones (Precept Austin):** After Jesus' busy activity in vv. 32–34, Mark takes us to the "power-room." Back of all the activities of the synagogue and the street lay a life of secret prayer. Jesus made time for prayer by giving up sleep. https://www.preceptaustin.org/quiet_time_seven_minutes_with_god
- **Same page:** It draws a call to a daily quiet time from Jesus' example. https://www.preceptaustin.org/quiet_time_seven_minutes_with_god

**vv. 36–39:** Nothing found.

**v. 40**
- **Guzik:** Lepers were treated as the "living dead." They had to cry "Unclean!" not because the disease spread easily, but because God used this disease as a striking example of sin and its effect on us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- **Guzik:** The man showed great faith, since as far as we know Jesus had not yet healed a leper. He asked to be *cleansed*, not just healed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- **Calvin:** By saying Christ was able to cleanse him if He was willing, the leper recognised divine power in Christ. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31.ix.lxx.html
- **Coffman:** The man did not ask Jesus to pray to God for him. He asked Jesus Himself to cleanse him, and he worshipped Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-40.html
- **Older commentary quoted on Bible Hub (probably the Pulpit Commentary, but I couldn't confirm):** "If thou wilt" shows the man accepted God's will. For bodily diseases are often necessary for the health of the soul; and this God knows, though man knows it not. https://biblehub.com/mark/1-40.htm

**Where teachers differ on "If You are willing": is it always God's will to heal?**
- **Bible.org (drawing on Ray Stedman):** Some people in the Charismatic movement claim that God always wants to heal us. But Jesus does not correct the leper when he says, "If you are willing ..." Scripture does not teach that everyone must be healed. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-cleansing-leper
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel; his Matthew 8 notes):** We should assume Jesus is willing to heal unless He shows us differently. He also says healing is an area where God especially shows His sovereignty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Mat/Mat_8.cfm
- **Seedbed (Wesleyan):** "If you are willing, you can make me clean" is a different prayer from "if it is your will, heal…" The first means going all in; the second means hedging your bet. https://seedbed.com/the-difference-between-if-its-your-will-and-if-you-are-willing/
- **Desiring God (Baptist):** Treats the healing as an example of "ask, and it will be given": The leper asked and the Lord gave. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/ask-god-is-willing-and-able-to-give-you-the-best-gifts
- I found no pages that set out the prosperity or word-of-faith view in its own words. The Bible.org line above is the only mention of the charismatic claim.

**v. 41**
- **Translation and manuscript question:**
  - The NIV reads "Jesus was indignant"; most translations say "moved with compassion." https://biblehub.com/niv/mark/1-41.htm
  - **Utley (Bible.org):** The Western Text, MS D, has "indignant," but MSS א, A, B, and C have "pity." The words are similar in Aramaic. The oldest and best manuscripts have "pity," but "indignant" would be the more unusual reading. https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-1
  - **NET Bible:** Keeps "compassion," the reading in almost every manuscript, but calls the decision difficult. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/download/netbible/ondemand/bybook/mar.pdf
- **The touch:**
  - **Guzik:** Jesus could have healed with a word, but chose to touch a man who had not felt a loving touch in years. He did not break the law, because the moment He touched him the man was no longer a leper. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
  - **Calvin:** The touch expressed compassion. The Son of God took our flesh to cleanse us and contracted no stain from it. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31.ix.lxx.html
  - **Barnes:** The touch shows Jesus already regarded him as clean. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-41.html
  - **Barclay:** To Jesus he was not unclean; he was simply a human soul in desperate need. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-41.html
  - **Strauss (TGC):** The touch is especially striking, since it would normally make a person ceremonially unclean. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/mark/

**v. 42**
- **Gill:** The cure seems to come from Jesus' spoken words rather than the touch, and it happened instantly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-42.html
- **Henry:** The cure was complete at once, with no sign of the leprosy left. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_001.cfm

**v. 43**
- **Constable:** The Greek word *embrimaomai* means a stern warning. Mark alone says compassion moved Jesus, and his account focuses on what the man did afterwards. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-42.html

**v. 44**
- **GotQuestions:** Only a priest could officially declare someone clean. In sending him, Jesus kept the law, restored the man to society and worship, and had the healing officially recorded. https://www.gotquestions.org/show-yourself-to-the-priest.html
- **Guzik:** The priests had probably never performed this ceremony. Looking it up and carrying it out would have been a strong sign that the Messiah was among them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-1/
- **Calvin:** All the honor that belonged to the ancient priests is now claimed by Christ alone as his own. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31.ix.lxx.html
- **The Bible Says (Blue Letter Bible):** "Tell no one" probably sets an order: the priest first, then others. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/mar-1-v40-45.cfm

**v. 45**
- **Constable:** The man's disobedience held back Jesus' mission instead of helping it. Since leprosy pictures sin, believers can easily see themselves in this cleansed sinner. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-41.html
- **Chuck Smith:** Jesus wanted more freedom of movement, but the news drew such crowds that He could no longer enter the towns. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/1-42.html
